name: Deep Freeze
dek: In Austin, you have four years to prepare for the February 2021 freeze. When residents turn up the heat, how much of your fleet will still be running?
description: Run Austin's public utility with four years to prepare for the February 2021 freeze. Would you winterize the plants you have or build backup power?
setup: You take over the public utility in 2017. Gas, coal, nuclear and wind all supply the city, and the cold can cut output from all four at once.
In this scenario you know the freeze is coming. You can retrofit the plants you have or keep the money for construction and individual upgrades.

decisions.title: Choose which plants to winterize
decisions.body: Check which plants already have winter protection before you spend money on the rest.

decisions.title: Check supply on a cold day
decisions.body: Look at which hours are short of power as heating demand rises. A backup plant that freezes too won't fill the gap.

decisions.title: Leave cash for gas
decisions.body: Winterizing a gas plant helps it keep running. You'll still have to buy its fuel when gas prices spike.

takeaway: How much would you spend before the first cold snap?

name: Data Center Boom
dek: Manassas has six years to get ready for 100 MW of new data centers. They'll need power all night. What will you run after sunset?
description: Run the Manassas grid as data centers ask for 100 MW. Take the developers' money for a 2026 connection or buy more time to build.
setup: In 2020, your municipal utility serves 16,500 customers with a gas peaker and an aging oil plant.

The developers offer to help pay for the full connection. Take the money and you'll need all 100 MW ready in January 2026. Turn it down and you can connect half then and the other half in January 2028.

decisions.title: Negotiate the connection
decisions.body: Compare the grant with the cost of getting new capacity ready by 2026. Phasing in the connection also delays half the new sales.

decisions.title: Cover the night shift
decisions.body: Look at demand after sunset. How much energy can you store during the day, and what will supply the rest?

decisions.title: Keep the city's customers
decisions.body: Check what residents pay while you build. If your rates drive them away, you lose sales from the people you already serve.

takeaway: Would you take the developers' money?

name: Carbon Fee
dek: San Francisco's coal plant has years left in it, but you pay a fee on its emissions. How soon can you afford to replace it?
description: A higher carbon fee is coming to San Francisco. Decide when your utility can afford to retire its coal plant and what should take its place.
setup: Your utility enters 2020 with an aging coal plant, a gas plant and a limited construction budget. Both plants pay a fee on emissions. The fee goes up in January 2024.
Your customers still need electricity while you build. If you close the coal plant first, check how much of that demand your gas plant can cover.

decisions.title: Work out what coal costs
decisions.body: Add the carbon fee to the cost of running each plant. Coal emits more per unit of electricity, so the higher fee hits it harder.

decisions.title: Time the retirement
decisions.body: Check your replacement's opening date before taking the old plant out of service.

decisions.title: Set a rate customers will pay
decisions.body: Raising prices can help pay for construction. Watch how many customers stay as their bills change.

takeaway: What will replace coal on your grid?

name: The Shale Boom
dek: A shale gas boom is coming to Pittsburgh. The fuel discount will end long before a new gas plant wears out.
description: Pittsburgh's shale boom makes gas cheap. Decide how much gas capacity to build when the discount may end before the plant has paid for itself.
setup: You begin in 2006 with a coal plant. As your utility grows, a regional gas glut makes a new gas plant an attractive way to meet demand.
During a winter freeze, gas gets more expensive just as gas plants produce less. When the boom ends, the regional discount disappears altogether.

decisions.title: Decide how much gas to build
decisions.body: Compare the fuel savings during the boom with what that same plant will cost you to run afterward.

decisions.title: Prepare for the freeze
decisions.body: Check which other plants can pick up the load if your gas units lose output at the same time.

decisions.title: Make room for new customers
decisions.body: Use the demand forecast to decide when to build. Keep enough cash to run the fleet you already own.

takeaway: How much of a twenty-year investment would you bet on cheap gas?

name: Paradise
dek: Honolulu has plenty of sun and wind. On a calm night, you're paying for imported oil. There's no neighboring grid to buy power from.
description: Run Honolulu's island grid on sun, wind and imported oil. Decide what will keep customers supplied on a calm night when the oil bill comes due.
setup: Take over an island utility in 2003. Its wind and solar farms already supply some electricity, but much of its capacity comes from an oil plant.
A delayed fuel shipment will push up oil prices. Every unit of electricity you can generate locally without oil is one less you have to pay that higher price for.

decisions.title: Decide what to build on the island
decisions.body: Compare the cost of a wind or solar project with the oil purchases it could save over its lifetime.

decisions.title: Save power for the evening
decisions.body: Look for hours when your wind and solar farms have electricity to spare. How much could you store for later?

decisions.title: Allow for visitors
decisions.body: Electricity use rises during the visitor boom. Check whether enough local supply will be ready for the extra demand.

takeaway: What would it take to burn less oil after sunset?

name: Rise of Renewables
dek: Wind and solar are getting cheaper in California. Waiting could save you money, but new factories will need power before long.
description: Wind and solar projects are getting cheaper in California. Can you wait for the discount and still have enough power when the factories open?
setup: You take over a San Francisco utility in 2002 with nuclear and oil plants. Over your twelve-year term, gas plants get cheaper to build, followed by solar and wind projects.
The lower construction prices apply to new orders. If you wait for a discount, check how much time you'll have left to build before factory demand rises.

decisions.title: Choose when to order
decisions.body: Check the forecast for equipment prices alongside the opening date for a new plant.

decisions.title: Cover the evening peak
decisions.body: Compare the hours your wind and solar projects produce power with the hours customers use it. What else needs to run then?

decisions.title: Pay the bills while you build
decisions.body: Until the new projects open, you're still paying for the oil your existing plant burns.

takeaway: Which project would you order first?

name: Hurricane Season
dek: A hurricane is coming to Puerto Rico. Several plants can lose output at once, and the oil you'll need during repairs gets more expensive.
description: Get San Juan's power grid ready for a hurricane. Several generators can lose output together, just when the island's oil gets more expensive.
setup: In 2000 you take over an island grid supplied by oil, gas and coal. You have several years before the 2008 hurricane season to decide what San Juan needs.
When the storm hits, some generators will produce less until repairs finish. The loss can be bigger than the spare capacity you'd normally keep for a single plant outage.

decisions.title: Build before landfall
decisions.body: Compare project completion dates with the storm outlook. New capacity needs to be ready while damaged plants are still under repair.

decisions.title: Plan for more than one outage
decisions.body: Look at what the rest of the fleet could supply if several of your generators lost output together.

decisions.title: Keep a fuel reserve in the budget
decisions.body: Check how much cash you'll need to keep the oil plants running at the higher price.

takeaway: How much backup can San Juan afford before the storm?

name: The End of an Era
dek: Two coal plants power your Pittsburgh utility. They're getting older, and a replacement can take years to build. Your customers can switch suppliers sooner than that.
description: Run a Pittsburgh utility with two aging coal plants. Decide which to replace first and how to keep customers supplied while you build.
setup: In 1980 you inherit coal plants of different ages. The older equipment will lose output, and new rules will eventually make coal more expensive to run.
Those plants also earn the revenue you need to replace them. You have twenty years to decide how long to run each one and what to build in its place.

decisions.title: Choose which plant to replace first
decisions.body: Look at each unit's age and output. Start the replacement early enough to supply customers when the old plant slows down.

decisions.title: Compare what the new plants can supply
decisions.body: Check both the construction price and the hours each project can cover. A cheap source of daytime power still leaves the night to plan for.

decisions.title: Keep customers through the change
decisions.body: Check the rates and reliability you're offering. Each customer who leaves takes some of your construction budget with them.

takeaway: When would you retire the first coal plant?

name: Heatwave + Drought
dek: Spain's hottest days are hard on both sides of your grid. People turn up the air conditioning just as drought cuts hydro output and warm rivers limit reactor cooling.
description: Run a scaled model of Spain's grid through four years of heat and drought. As demand for cooling rises, both dams and reactors lose output.
setup: Your four-year term starts in 2023 with a scaled version of Spain's national fleet. You have wind, solar, gas and a battery alongside the dams and reactors.
During a hot, dry summer, less water flows into your reservoirs. Your reactors can also lose output even when they have plenty of fuel.

decisions.title: Watch the water coming in
decisions.body: Check how quickly the reservoir is refilling. Its level today tells you how much water you have, but the inflow determines how long it will last.

decisions.title: Cover both losses
decisions.body: Look at the hours when hydro and nuclear output fall together. Compare new supply with storing electricity or reducing demand in those hours.

decisions.title: Price the backup
decisions.body: Gas can fill a shortfall. Check what it adds to your fuel bill and emissions before relying on it for the whole summer.

takeaway: What will supply the grid when the rivers run low?

name: Sudden Nuclear Shutdown
dek: Your largest reactor supplies much of your Paris utility's power. Sometime during your five-year term it will shut down and stay offline.
description: Your Paris utility's largest reactor will shut down. See what the rest of the fleet can supply and decide how much backup to build before it happens.
setup: You start with the reactor, wind and solar farms, a small gas peaker and a battery. You know the shutdown is coming, but you don't know the exact month.
Pause the game, then pause the reactor. The supply chart will show you when the remaining fleet falls short.

decisions.title: Measure the gap
decisions.body: Check how much electricity is missing at night as well as during the day. That tells you what a replacement needs to deliver.

decisions.title: Size the backup
decisions.body: Compare a new generator with more storage. If you choose batteries, check that you'll have enough surplus electricity to charge them.

decisions.title: Decide when to build
decisions.body: Paying for extra capacity early ties up cash. Wait too long and you may still be building when the reactor shuts down.

takeaway: Could your utility get through tomorrow without its biggest reactor?

name: Wildfire Emergency
dek: Wildfire will cut your Los Angeles utility's main power connection to a tenth of its usual capacity. What can you have ready by January 2025?
description: Wildfire cuts a Los Angeles utility's northern power connection by 90% for two months. Choose what will replace the imports in January and February 2025.
setup: In this fictional utility, you start in 2022 with gas, solar, wind and a battery. Northern imports help cover the hours when those local sources fall short.
The scenario gives you advance warning. In January and February 2025, your existing northern connection will lose 90% of its capacity.

decisions.title: Measure the missing imports
decisions.body: Look at the hours when you buy the most power from the north. Check what the same connection could deliver during the fire.

decisions.title: Choose a second source
decisions.body: Compare the cost and lead time of local generation with building an independent connection.

decisions.title: Check the hours after sunset
decisions.body: Batteries can store surplus solar power for the evening. Check how long they'll last before imports have to make up the difference.

takeaway: Where would you get two months of replacement power?

name: Load Shedding
dek: Coal plants in your Johannesburg utility are breaking down faster than they can be repaired. Diesel can keep the lights on, if you can pay the fuel bill.
description: Coal plants keep breaking down in South Africa. Decide what to build before the utility spends its cash on diesel to cover the shortages.
setup: You take over in 2016 with a scaled version of South Africa's fleet. Alongside coal, you have a little nuclear, diesel, wind and solar generation.
Breakdowns leave you with less coal power each year. Diesel can cover some of the shortfall while you build, but every delay means buying more fuel.

decisions.title: Plan around the plants that still work
decisions.body: Check how much coal power is actually available before deciding how much new capacity to order.

decisions.title: Budget for diesel
decisions.body: Work out how long you'll need emergency generation before a replacement opens. Can the utility afford to run it for that long?

decisions.title: Check the replacement after dark
decisions.body: Look for hours when the new fleet still falls short. If those gaps remain, you'll still need the diesel plant.

takeaway: How soon can you give the diesel generators a break?

name: The River Runs Dry
dek: Zambia's Copperbelt mines draw power around the clock. The reservoir on the Zambezi starts full, but an El Niño drought is coming.
description: A drought is coming to Zambia's hydro-dependent grid. Use the time a full reservoir buys you to find power for Copperbelt mines that run around the clock.
setup: Your utility starts in 2012 with a hydro plant, a small diesel plant and a little solar. The dam supplies most of your electricity.
When inflow falls, each release uses water the river is slow to replace. The diesel plant is too small to take over when the reservoir runs low.

decisions.title: Use the time the reservoir buys you
decisions.body: Watch the inflow forecast while the lake is still full. That's when you have time to build another source of power.

decisions.title: Compare alternatives to hydro
decisions.body: Check how much electricity a new plant would supply during a dry spell and what it would cost to run.

decisions.title: Keep the mines supplied overnight
decisions.body: Compare solar output with the industrial load. Work out what would keep the mines running between sunset and sunrise.

takeaway: What would you build while the dam still has water?

name: Delhi Summer
dek: Delhi's air conditioners need more power each summer. In the heat of 2024, coal and gas plants will produce less, and a late monsoon will prolong the shortage risk.
description: Prepare Delhi's utility for hotter summers through 2024. Air conditioners draw more power just as high temperatures cut coal and gas output.
setup: You take over in 2018 with coal, gas, solar, wind and a small battery. Over seven years, each summer pushes demand higher.
Hot weather cuts the output of your coal and gas plants just when customers need them most. Look at which hours run short before you decide how to prepare.

decisions.title: Build between summers
decisions.body: Check how much spare power you had at last year's peak. Will the next project finish before that margin is gone?

decisions.title: Stretch solar past sunset
decisions.body: Look for spare daytime solar power you could store. Check how long the battery can cover cooling demand into the evening.

decisions.title: Reduce the peak
decisions.body: Compare what it costs to reduce electricity use during a hot spell with the cost of running another plant.

takeaway: How much cooling demand can you cover if the monsoon is late?

name: Across the Valley
dek: Buy three neighboring utilities by December 2014. Once the deals close, their customers expect you to keep the lights on too.
description: Buy three neighboring utilities by December 2014 in a fictional Vermont power market. Can your expanded company supply all the customers it inherits?
setup: In 2005 you run Champlain Electric, a fictional utility around Burlington, Vermont. The neighbors you can buy come with equipment, debts and contracts to purchase power.
You still have to run the larger network after the acquisition deadline. Upkeep rises, and the limits on purchased power get tighter in 2017 and again in 2020.

decisions.title: Read the purchase terms
decisions.body: Compare each company's debt and contracts alongside its asking price. How much cash will you have left after the deal closes?

decisions.title: Check the connections
decisions.body: See how much power each connection can carry before counting on a neighboring plant to cover a shortage.

decisions.title: Replace the purchased power
decisions.body: Check how much supply the contracts will still cover in 2017. Allow time to build replacements while you're paying for network upkeep.

takeaway: Which neighbor would you buy first?

name: Chernobyl: Recovery
dek: In March 1986, all four Chernobyl reactors are producing electricity. A month from now, all four will be offline. Part of your job is paying for the cleanup.
description: Run a regional grid through five years of recovery after Chernobyl. Restore electricity as the surviving reactors return and pay for cleanup at Unit 4.
setup: You run a model of the regional grid, with coal and oil plants alongside the reactors. After the April disaster, Units 1 and 2 return that fall. Unit 3 stays offline until December 1987. Unit 4 never returns.
Your term runs through February 1991. Blackouts cost you points and you can keep working to restore service afterward. Bankruptcy ends the run.

decisions.title: Restore service between restarts
decisions.body: Compare what the coal and oil plants can supply now with what new construction could deliver before the surviving reactors return.

decisions.title: Pay for cleanup
decisions.body: Unit 4 carries a monthly cleanup bill. You can't sell the reactor, so keep that expense in your budget even after the other units restart.

decisions.title: Track what customers experience
decisions.body: At the end of five years, review the service you restored, what customers paid and the emissions your grid produced.

takeaway: How much service can you restore with the resources you have?

name: First Light (1882–1901)
dek: It's 1882. You own one small coal plant and sell electricity to 100 customers. Can you get their payments to cover the cost of keeping the plant running?
description: Start a California utility in 1882 with a small coal plant and 100 customers. By the end of year four, electricity sales need to cover operating costs.
setup: First Light begins the Legacy campaign in a fictional California utility. You'll run the same company from 1882 to 2061, handing it on after each twenty-year term.
Your first deadline is four years away. By then, electricity sales need to cover your operating costs. After that, you'll have a growing customer base to supply.

decisions.title: Set your first price
decisions.body: How much do you need to charge to pay the coal bill? Watch what happens to your customer count as you change the rate.

decisions.title: Consider river power
decisions.body: A small hydro site becomes available in 1895. Compare what it costs to build with the coal you could save.

decisions.title: Plan the first handover
decisions.body: The next generation starts with your customers and equipment. It also takes over any debt you leave behind.

takeaway: What kind of company will those first 100 customers help you build?

name: Beyond the Dynamo (1902–1921)
dek: More people want electricity from the company you started in First Light. How many new customers can the old plants serve before you have to borrow for another one?
description: Take over the company you built in First Light. Grow its customer base through 1921 without leaving the next generation more debt than it can handle.
setup: In 1902 you take over the same California utility you ran through the first generation. Its opening fleet and bank balance depend on what you did with those first twenty years.
Your goal is to grow the customer base by the end of 1921. Check how much extra demand the inherited fleet can meet before you order new capacity.

decisions.title: Make room for new customers
decisions.body: Check when demand is closest to available supply. That's where new customers will first put pressure on the old plants.

decisions.title: Finance the next plant
decisions.body: Compare the extra revenue new customers could bring with the cost of borrowing to serve them. Any debt still outstanding in 1921 passes to your successor.

takeaway: Which of your first investments still has room to grow?

name: Affordable Growth (1922–1941)
dek: Your California utility has more customers now. They need enough new capacity to meet rising demand, at a rate they can still afford.
description: Inherit a growing California utility in 1922. Build enough power for the customers you serve while keeping their electricity rate within the 1941 target.
setup: In 1922 you take over the company you built in Beyond the Dynamo. The plants have aged another twenty years, and any debt you've taken on still needs to be paid.
At the end of 1941, the campaign checks the rate you actually billed your customers. Check the target before you decide how much to spend on construction.

decisions.title: Compare the running costs
decisions.body: Look at what a new project's fuel and upkeep would add to each bill, alongside the cost to build it.

decisions.title: Decide how much to borrow
decisions.body: If new capacity opens too soon, you're paying for equipment that sits idle. Check the demand forecast before committing to a loan.

decisions.title: Set the rate
decisions.body: Compare the target with what you're charging. Can you afford the next round of construction at that rate?

takeaway: What would your customers pay for a kilowatt-hour in 1941?

name: Everybody Plugs In (1942–1961)
dek: More California homes and businesses are plugging in. Halfway through your term you'll need spare power on top of what they're already using.
description: Run your California utility from 1942 to 1961. Growing electricity demand leaves less room to spare, and you'll need a reserve by the end of year eleven.
setup: You take over in 1942, sixty years after the company opened. Your starting fleet is the one the previous generation left you.
By the end of year eleven, you need spare capacity equal to 10% of the peak demand you started with. Demand grows while your crews are building.

decisions.title: Build ahead of the checkpoint
decisions.body: Check how long each project takes. A plant that opens after year eleven won't count toward that reserve.

decisions.title: Choose how to pay for spare capacity
decisions.body: Compare the cost of adding another plant with the extra demand you expect it to serve. Your successor will inherit both the plant and the financing.

takeaway: How much spare power will you have when the new customers arrive?

name: The Power You Don't Build (1962–1981)
dek: The oil shocks of the 1970s are coming. If your customers can use less electricity, your California utility can buy less fuel.
description: Take a California utility through the oil shocks of 1973 and 1979. By 1981, efficiency programs need to save 5% of home and business electricity use.
setup: In 1962 you inherit the plants your earlier generations chose. If much of the fleet runs on oil, the price shocks of 1973 and 1979 will hit your fuel bill harder.
By the end of 1981, your efficiency programs need to save 5% of home and business electricity use.

decisions.title: Compare efficiency with new supply
decisions.body: Estimate how much electricity a program would save before committing to another plant. Those savings can also reduce the fuel you buy today.

decisions.title: Check the oil bill
decisions.body: Look at how often your oil plants run and what else could supply those hours if fuel gets expensive.

decisions.title: Measure the savings
decisions.body: Check how much the programs actually cut household and business use. That tells you how far you are from the 5% goal.

takeaway: How much fuel could you save by helping customers use less electricity?

name: The Price of Power (1982–2001)
dek: Regional power has helped supply your California utility. From July 2000, the northern connection won't be able to bring in as much.
description: Prepare for eighteen months of restricted northern power imports, starting in July 2000. Keep a month of operating costs in cash during the crisis.
setup: This sixth generation starts in 1982. Near the end of your term, northern imports will be limited for eighteen months. How much local power you'll need depends on what you inherited.
During the crisis, the campaign also checks whether you have a month's operating costs in cash. Money tied up in a new plant won't pay those bills.

decisions.title: Measure your reliance on imports
decisions.body: Check northern purchases during your busiest hours. Use that gap to size local backup or another connection.

decisions.title: Keep cash for the crisis
decisions.body: Look at a month's operating expenses before you place a construction order. Will that much still be in the bank during the squeeze?

takeaway: Can you afford both the backup power and the cash reserve?

name: The Sun Moves the Peak (2002–2021)
dek: Solar can cover a sunny California afternoon. This generation's goal is to serve 99.5% of evening demand, when solar output is falling.
description: Run a California utility through 2021. A wildfire will restrict imports that summer, and you need to serve 99.5% of evening demand at the end of your term.
setup: You take over in 2002 with the utility you built through six previous generations. Check the supply chart near sunset to see what still runs when daytime output falls.
A wildfire will restrict northern imports in July and August 2021. The evening service check comes in the last month of your term.

decisions.title: Shift daytime power into the evening
decisions.body: If you have a midday surplus, check how much you could store and how long it would last after sunset.

decisions.title: Prepare for the wildfire
decisions.body: Compare local supply with what another connection could carry while northern imports are restricted.

decisions.title: Lower emissions after dark
decisions.body: Check which plants actually run in the evening. That's where a cleaner replacement could help you meet demand and cut emissions at the same time.

takeaway: What will supply your grid at sunset?

name: Renew the Grid (2022–2041)
dek: Which oil plants are still running after seven generations? It's 2022, and any you kept from 2000 or earlier will need to retire as California's demand grows.
description: Run a California utility through 2041. Older oil plants lose output in 2030, and you need to replace the units that went into service by 2000.
setup: When 2030 arrives, oil equipment that's at least thirty years old drops to 60% output. How much power you lose depends on what you built and kept in earlier terms.
By the end of year fourteen, you need to retire oil equipment commissioned in 2000 or earlier. Check the commissioning dates before you put in the first replacement order.

decisions.title: Find the units due to retire
decisions.body: See how much power those units supply today. You may have already replaced some of them in an earlier chapter.

decisions.title: Time the replacements
decisions.body: Compare opening dates with the output cut in 2030 and the retirement deadline. Demand will keep growing while the fleet changes over.

decisions.title: Decide what to pass on
decisions.body: Check what the new equipment will cost customers and what it will emit. The last generation of your company will inherit those plants and any debt.

takeaway: How much old oil capacity will you still depend on in 2030?

name: A Different Kind of Growth (2042–2061)
dek: Your last twenty years come with one carbon budget. Every tonne your California utility emits in 2042 counts toward the same total as a tonne in 2061.
description: Finish Electrify's Legacy campaign in 2061. As demand grows, keep your California utility within one carbon budget for the entire twenty-year term.
setup: Eight generations have handed this company on. In 2042 you take over their fleet and finances for the ninth and final term.
Electricity demand keeps growing. An early cut in emissions gives you more room in the budget for years when you need extra generation.

decisions.title: Choose which emissions to cut first
decisions.body: Look at which plants run most often. Bringing a cleaner replacement online early saves emissions for more of the term.

decisions.title: Look at the whole day's demand
decisions.body: Compare building capacity with helping customers use less. Check whether the resulting fleet can still cover the hours after sunset.

decisions.title: Keep the company running through 2061
decisions.body: Track bills and debt alongside the carbon total. Customers still need reliable power throughout your final term.

takeaway: Can you take the utility that started with one coal plant all the way to 2061?
